set.approach: Park at the pullouts on Highway 120 (Tioga Road) just over half a mile east of Ellery Lake dam, or use the Warren Creek trailhead area nearby, and climb the broken slabs above the road straight up to the base of the ridge. The first climbing is a steep, loose dihedral.
set.descent_text: From the top there are several ways down. You can downclimb west on ledges to the small brushy basin on the backside, or downclimb the notch toward the highway (class 4 to 5, with route-finding). Retracing the ridge crux is a further option.

review.notes: Route page (listed as Northeast Ridge, URL east-ridge, 5.7, 12 pitches) for the descent options and the dihedral; area page for the road parking and slabs. No counts given.

set.approach: The wall stands directly above Spring Lake at the head of Cliff Creek Canyon, in the backcountry of Sequoia and Kings Canyon, and every way in starts at the Mineral King road end. The usual line is to hike to Monarch Lake and cross Glacier Pass into the basin; the other choice is to go over Timber Gap and then follow Cliff Creek up to the lake. Spring Roll begins at the toe of the left-most of the three formations that make up the wall.
set.descent_text: Walk off the back of the formation, skier's left, heading down toward Cyclamen Lake. A short rappel from a slung boulder into a steep gully may be needed; staying higher and further left may allow a scramble instead. Continue left and down through the slabs to return to Spring Lake. Another option is to go on up to the top of the main formation and descend by its line.

review.notes: Approach: area page (both access options) and the route page / AAJ note agree on Mineral King start and the toe of the left-most formation. Descent: route page only; no counts given.

set.approach: The Paradise Ridge trailhead sits off the Mineral King road, near Atwell Mill; hike that trail up to the ridge crest. From there go cross-country north-northwest, contouring across minor drainages until the Fortress wall, with its gully below, shows ahead. Keep to the gully's east (right) bank until you are beneath the wall, then step across and scramble up to the foot of the rock. The Sage is the left-most route on the wall.

review.notes: Approach line from the Fortress area page; AAJ note supports the brushy burned approach. Distances left out (one source). No descent source for this route.

ca_tuttle_slab_jim_s_buttress.skip_reason: identity in doubt: the only page describing it places it on the south side of Tuttle Creek, across from the slab whose access is documented

set.approach: Start on the Tuttle Creek trail and walk to the stone landmark called the Ashram, then bear left along a sandy sidehill path to reach the south fork of the creek and follow that drainage uphill. The path fades past the Ashram, so watch for cairns. Some way up, the Tuttle Creek Obelisk appears above on the right; keep going until the creek runs directly beneath the Basecamp Wall below the Obelisk. The wall is clean, with camping and water at its foot. An overnight wilderness permit is needed to camp in Tuttle Creek.

review.notes: Wall page lists this as the only climb; no line position or descent given. Distances left out (one source).

set.approach: Leave the car at the pack station where the Pine Creek road ends and take the Pine Creek Pass trail uphill; the Brownstone Mine wall appears on the left, a short step off the trail, so no off-trail travel is needed. The trail is sunny even though the wall is shaded, so an early start helps, and early in the season there are several creek crossings with little water at the crag itself. Alpine Creek is one of the longer lines in the Upper Brownstone section of the crag.

review.notes: Shared crag access from the area page; Upper Brownstone listing names Alpine Creek. No distance given (the two pages repeat one wording).
